title: A Chief Minister Bent on Holding Closing Ceremonies!
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement. Letter-specific notes: - The English newspaper quotations are reproduced exactly as printed in the Tamil source, including capitalisation and syntax. - Project costs, land-area figures and attributed legal submissions are translated as presented in the letter without external reconciliation.
paragraphs: I have spoken many times about the Maduravoyal–Port elevated expressway project. On 8 January 2009, the Honourable Prime Minister, Dr Manmohan Singh, came in person and laid its foundation stone in my presence. The work was progressing rapidly when the Tamil Nadu Government obstructed it. On 14 August, I wrote in detail in Murasoli about the projects worth many crores that would arise in the area if the road were completed; the efforts made by the National Highways Authority of India to continue it; and the contractor’s case demanding ₹873 crore in compensation from the NHAI.

As I had urged, the Tiruvallur, North Chennai and South Chennai district units of the DMK organised a massive protest at Nerkundram on 17 August 2013. Although the ruling party denied permission and made arrests, the protest was held.

The Tamil Nadu Government delayed filing its counter-affidavit in court. After the High Court imposed a deadline, newspapers carried photographs showing that the Chief Minister had reviewed the project with officials. Yet even after that review, the Government made no announcement indicating that the project would continue. Instead, it decided to press the NHAI to examine alternatives that would not obstruct floodwater during the monsoon along the already planned alignment.

Customs agents and trade organisations have stressed that the Chennai Port–Maduravoyal elevated road is not merely a port-development project. It would ease city congestion and support the State’s industrial and economic growth; therefore, they say, the State Government must remove its obstruction.

Chennai Port handles 15 lakh containers a year, with about 4,000 container lorries entering and leaving every day. Police officers themselves believe that inadequate roads cause congestion, accidents and deaths. This project was designed as the solution. T.K.A. Nair, Adviser to the Prime Minister, and Union Secretary A.K. Upadhyay came to Chennai and held discussions with the Tamil Nadu Chief Secretary. Yet every effort by the NHAI ended in failure.
This is not the only project. I have repeatedly explained how many schemes begun during the DMK Government have been paralysed by the AIADMK Government.

In July 2012, the NHAI approved a ₹617-crore project to construct a four-lane road over 54 kilometres between Coimbatore and Mettupalayam. Preliminary work had begun. The Tamil Nadu Government was required to sign an agreement to cooperate with the scheme, but it did not do so, delaying land acquisition. Meanwhile tenders were called and a work order was issued. The State Government then demanded that the proposed toll-plaza site be shifted, later asked for another boundary location and imposed several further conditions. After waiting patiently, the NHAI decided to abandon the Coimbatore–Mettupalayam four-lane project itself.
On 28 August 2013, The Hindu published a detailed report on page five. It began:

In what could be its first salvo at the State Government, the National Highways Authority of India on Tuesday withdrew from a Project to extend National Highway-67 in Coimbatore District between Kangeyampalayam to Mettupalayam. A top NHAI official described it as the first step towards the national agency withdrawing from Tamil Nadu. This decision could have a bearing on major projects in Tamil Nadu, where the NHAI alleges it is encountering a series of hurdles from the State Government

In substance, the NHAI withdrew the Kangeyampalayam–Mettupalayam road project because of its dispute with the State Government. A senior NHAI official described it as the first step towards the national agency withdrawing from Tamil Nadu and warned that the decision could affect major projects in the State because of the repeated obstacles encountered from the State Government.
Thus, for lack of cooperation from the AIADMK Government, the NHAI has now abandoned this project.

Likewise, during the DMK Government, a decision was taken in April 2009 to build a 620-metre flyover at the Oragadam junction, where the Singaperumal Koil–Sriperumbudur and Vandalur–Walajabad roads meet, to reduce traffic congestion. The ₹20.89-crore work was entrusted to the company undertaking East Coast Road construction. Reports now say that work there too is moving extremely slowly. Is the reason once again that the flyover was begun during the DMK Government?

Next, the NHAI undertook the upgrading of about 107 kilometres of highway between Tiruchi and Karaikudi at an estimated cost of ₹374 crore. Begun under the DMK Government on 12 July 2010, it should have been completed by May this year. The Tamil Nadu Government had already issued a no-objection certificate. When 90 per cent of the work had been completed and the road was nearing public use, the AIADMK Government ordered that the certificate be withdrawn. Because that order was against public welfare, the NHAI approached the High Court seeking its cancellation.

Counsel for the Tamil Nadu Government argued that the certificate was properly withdrawn because the road work would affect water bodies along the route. Additional Solicitor-General P. Wilson, appearing for the NHAI, submitted that Anna University had found that the project would not harm water bodies. A team of IIT Madras experts had also reported that it would provide many benefits and would cause no such damage. He therefore asked the Court to cancel the Government’s withdrawal of approval for a project benefiting lakhs of people. Judgment has been reserved.

Land acquisition for the Salem–Ulundurpet National Highway project began under the DMK Government in 2009. For the widening of 136 kilometres of highway, 19,000 acres of agricultural land were acquired, and the Highways Department allocated ₹250 crore as compensation. Farmers demanded compensation at market value and filed a case in the Madras High Court.

The Salem and Villupuram District Collectors were directed to take action to pay proper compensation by December 2012, but no action was taken. In the High Court, the farmers alleged that the Salem Collector was demanding a 30 per cent commission. The Court censured the Collector. The farmers have announced a protest demanding compensation for the acquired land.

As another achievement of the AIADMK Government, today’s Hindu—3 September 2013—reported under the headline, “Proposal for flyover on Pantheon Road scrapped - Decision taken as consultant says it would be unfeasible; Proposed flyovers at PH Road, Arcot Road to be re-designed with more ramps.” The Chennai Corporation has decided to abandon the proposed Pantheon Road flyover after a consultant called it unfeasible, and to redesign the proposed flyovers on Poonamallee High Road and Arcot Road.

Another report in the same newspaper states that the NHAI has not begun any major project in Tamil Nadu during the past two years. The first major project to be halted was the Chennai Port–Maduravoyal elevated road, conceived at a cost of ₹1,815 crore to move containers quickly from Maduravoyal. The Public Works Department stopped it last year, alleging that the work departed from the approved design. The contractor has meanwhile demanded ₹873 crore in compensation. A senior Union Government official reportedly said that it was a good project capable of relieving congestion at Chennai Port and that its loss would seriously affect the State and the national economy. The official also said that, should the State Government wish to take it up, the Centre was ready to resume it and hoped the differences would soon be resolved.

The NHAI is not the private responsibility of any individual; it is an agency of the Union Government. Projects worth many crores must be implemented through it in Tamil Nadu. It is not right to stop each project, after crores have already been spent, by advancing one reason or another. Those entrusted with governing Tamil Nadu should argue for and obtain more projects from the Union Government and then implement them in the State. They should not halt each one out of political rancour.

What benefit has come from keeping the buildings at the Omandurar Government Estate closed for three years merely because they were constructed during the DMK Government, while the administration continues at the old Secretariat because of the Chief Minister’s obstinacy? Last month, part of a wall there fell and injured a woman, who was taken to hospital. Yesterday, a fire caused by an electrical fault at the Secretariat was fortunately averted. The Chief Minister should at least now consider all this and reach a sound decision—for her own good and for the good of the State.
But if she continues to insist that the hare she caught has only three legs, Tamil Nadu will inevitably have to face the consequences.
With affection, M.K.
4 September 2013
